content:
I just published my complete guide to reinforcement learning for LLMs. It's a single, standalone resource for understanding RL from first principles to frontier research.

Read it here: https://t.co/iUMAWUrkQ1

The topics covered are as follows…

RL Fundamentals:
- A general framework for RL (policy, states, actions, transition functions, environment, rewards, trajectories, etc.)
- Core concepts of RL (returns, discounting, action / state / trajectory probabilities, value / advantage functions).
- Formulating and estimating the learning objective for RL.

Basic of RL for LLMs:
- Token-level (MDP) vs. completion-level (bandit) formulations.
- Outcome versus process rewards.
- Value estimation via value models / critics.
- KL divergence, RL setups (RLHF, RLVR, infra, etc.), importance sampling.

Basic Policy Gradients:
- Deriving the RL objective / vanilla policy gradient (VPG) from first principles.
- Different policy-gradient formulations (trajectory returns, reward-to-go, baselines, value functions, and advantages).
- Why policy gradient estimates have high variance (and how baselines help).
- Implementation of VPG.

REINFORCE and its variants:
- REINFORCE as a Monte Carlo implementation of the VPG.
- Completion-level vs. token-level implementations of REINFORCE.
- Reward baselines and KL-regularized rewards.
- RLOO, REINFORCE++ and other critic-free policy gradient algorithms.

Actor-Critic Methods:
- Training value models / critics alongside the policy to estimate advantages.
- Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) and KL-constrained policy updates.
- How PPO simplifies TRPO with a clipped surrogate objective.
- Full PPO details (clipping, advantage estimations, value loss, KL, policy ratios, multi-epoch optimization, etc.) + implementation.
- Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) + implementation.
- The memory and computational overhead of actor-critic algorithms.

GRPO:
- Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) as a simpler alternative to PPO.
- Group-relative advantage estimates + implementation.
- Why removing the critic is helpful.
- Limitations of vanilla GRPO algorithm.
- Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GSPO, and other recent improvements.

Recent research topics:
- Online versus offline RL.
- Rubric-based RL.
- RL scaling laws.
- Agentic RL + world modeling.

This post is a synthesis of my writing / learning on RL for over a year. I hope it’s helpful!

title:
I’m stunned. 

“Does G_2/SU(3) = S^6 admit an upgrade from almost complex to honest complex structure? “

This problem is part of an orphaned cluster of octonionic sphere transitive phenomena involvin
content:
I’m stunned. 

“Does G_2/SU(3) = S^6 admit an upgrade from almost complex to honest complex structure? “

This problem is part of an orphaned cluster of octonionic sphere transitive phenomena involving G_2, and Spin(n! For the values n=7,8 and 9. 

To put it in a setting. It’s not really about the 6 dimensional sphere. It’s about a larger question that nobody seems to ask directly about “Number”.

Assume that in a certain sense there are provably only 4 possible systems of numbers with proper addition/subtraction and multiplication/division. 

They spel out the Hindi word for thief or: C-H-O-R, where C stands for complex numbers, R for real numbers and H for Hamilton’s quaternioniv numbers. 

In the 1950s, my friend Raoul Bott found a repeating pattern which when stylized looks like 

-R-R-R-C-H-H-H-C-R-R-R-C-H-H-H-C-R-R-R-C-H-H-H-C-R-R-R-C-H-H-

And naively it looks O or the octonionic numbers don’t participate. But if you stare at it a little bit harder, you see that the basic sequence is 8 letters in length and O is suspiciously of dimension 8. 

This leads to a question that I consider the most exciting pure math question I know: Are the octonionic O at the center of pure mathematics or are they a freakish system excluded from the core of pure mathematics and banished to the periphery?  This is not a mainstream concern, and the only two leading mathematicians I ever heard share this sentiment directly were Jean-Pierre Serre and Bert Kostant. Serre once theatrically shut the office door and called it something only to be whispered about late at night in hushed tones. 

More or less, the world of pure mathematics treats O like the crazy relative no one understands. And Serre, Kostant, myself and a small minority treat it as somehow CENTRAL to pure mathematics in a way no one fully grasps. I’m sorry to say that Raoul disagreed with me on this. At least in public. 

This Claude result comes from that seditious line of thought. G_2 is the symmetry of the O numbers and the 6 sphere lives in their 7 dimensional imaginary component within the full 8-dimensional system. 

But a complex structure is part of normal math. 

So you can read this as “AI just found a bridge between the freakish 6-sphere and the octoniond and the normal mathematics of complex structures within R, C and H.”

I’m totally shaken. This is huge.

title:
Electricity reached factories in 1882. Factory productivity didn't move for almost 40 years. The motor was never the bottleneck, and the same thing is happening to AI right now.

Edison's Pearl Street
content:
Electricity reached factories in 1882. Factory productivity didn't move for almost 40 years. The motor was never the bottleneck, and the same thing is happening to AI right now.

Edison's Pearl Street station opened in New York in 1882. By 1899, electric motors powered less than 5% of machinery in American factories. A skeptic in 1900 could point at the dynamo and say it was everywhere except the productivity statistics. He'd have been right.

The reason is the shape of the building.

Steam factories ran off one giant engine turning a central shaft, with belts and pulleys dragging power to every machine. Everything had to sit close to the engine, so factories were stacked five stories high around it, and the machines were arranged by distance to the shaft rather than by the order work actually flowed.

When electricity arrived, owners did the obvious thing. They pulled out the steam engine, bolted a big electric motor to the same shaft, and kept everything else. Same belts, same layout, same workflow. Economists call it group drive. It saved a little coal and changed nothing.

The gains only showed up in the 1920s, when a new generation of factories put a small motor inside every machine. That let them tear out the shafts, spread onto a single floor, and lay the machines out in the order the product moved. Manufacturing productivity grew more than 5% a year through that decade. Electricity accounted for roughly half of it. Four decades after the plug went in.

Now run the last three years through that lens. GPT-4 arrived and every company did group drive. They hooked a chatbot to a workflow designed for humans and kept the org chart, the approval chain, and the software stack exactly as they were. That is why the disruption Sam expected never showed up on schedule. Nobody rebuilt the floor.

Unit drive for AI means rebuilding the process around the agent instead of the person, and that requires ripping out working systems that still make money. In 1900 no owner would scrap a serviceable plant to find out. In 2026 no CIO will scrap a serviceable Salesforce instance either.

The technology is ahead of Sam's 2023 timeline. The buildings are 30 years behind it.

content:
For years, the advice was to move to San Francisco if you wanted a career in tech. That advice is now wrong. New York has become the most exciting place in the world to build.

A few reasons why:

1. The AI labs are here. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and hundreds of others all run meaningful operations in NYC.  You can now build a serious frontier-tech career here without giving up anything.
 
2. Every major industry lives here, and so does its AI counterpart. New York doesn't only have "tech," but finance, media, advertising, fashion, healthcare, real estate, law, and commerce too, with their applied-AI layer counterparts being built on top of each one. 
 
3. The talent pool is unlike anywhere else. SF gives you engineers. New York gives you engineers, plus world-class designers, salespeople, bankers, marketers, operators, creatives, and media people, all at the top of their fields. Companies will need all of them.
 
4. People actually want to live here. New York is unlike any other city with its density of restaurants, art, nightlife, fashion, and media - and the people working across these sectors.
 
If you're building something and you're more than just tech, I'd argue there's only one city for you right now.

A few months ago, he was one of the most bullish people I knew on AI semis. This week, he looked honestly confused and upset. 

He told me, maybe there’s no beta left in this sector. His biggest concern wasn’t supply chain, it was downstream demand. Specifically, Anthropic’s reported ARR. Some numbers floating around are way below what bulls expected, and if model revenue growth is slowing, the whole AI CapEx cycle gets questioned. But here’s the disconnect. He said that every time he talks to suppliers or people closer to the supply chain, it’s the opposite. Orders are strong, expansion continues, everyone close to the supply chain still sounds extremely bullish. 

My response to him was that this is indeed bearish noise short term before the Anthropic IPO as it’s guilty until proven innocent, but for the long term investors these feel more narrative driven than structural: I think Anthropic is managing the expectation before IPO, and the growth number conflicts among multiple sources and seasonality also muddies the ARR reads(don’t forget the ChatGPT DAU read last year)
Even if Anthropic’s growth rate peaks due to the supply constraints it doesn’t necessarily mean the whole AI sector slows down in terms of the monetization (look at Codex’s insane WAU growth!)

So, two coWe also talked about U.S. politics. There’s clearly more pushback on data centers around power, water, and noise. My take is that the market is probably overpricing that risk into midterms. assuming a real slowdown in build-out. I think that’s too pessimistic. My response to him was that these feel more narrative driven than structural. Management teams are cautious pre-IPO. Data sources conflict, and competition muddies simple ARR reads. Before midterms and the Anthropic IPO, sentiment could stay weak across semis and AI infrastructure. And after those milestones, we may finally get clarity on actual demand and political impact. If fundamentals hold, this stretch of uncertainty could end up looking like a buying opp.

content:
AI is not one technology.

It’s an entire ecosystem.

And the deeper you go, the more you realize that ChatGPT or Claude is only one layer of a much bigger stack.

At the foundation, you have:

→ Machine learning
→ Neural networks
→ Transformers
→ Computer vision
→ Large language models

Then comes the infrastructure that makes these models useful:

→ Data & knowledge systems
→ Fine-tuning
→ Prompt engineering
→ RAG
→ Knowledge graphs
→ Model serving & inference

But that’s still not the end.

The next layer is where AI starts doing things:

→ AI agents
→ Tool orchestration
→ Multi-agent systems
→ Autonomous execution
→ Memory systems
→ Self-reflection & error recovery

And then AI moves into real-world applications:

→ AI copilots
→ Personalization
→ Content generation
→ Code generation
→ Voice & video
→ Business automation

But there’s one part that becomes more important as AI gets more autonomous:

Trust.

Security.
Privacy.
Bias & fairness.
Explainability.
Human oversight.
Risk management.
Governance.
Compliance.

Because building a powerful AI system is only half the problem.

The bigger challenge is building one that people can trust, control and deploy safely.

That’s why the future of AI isn’t just about better models.

It’s about the entire ecosystem working together.

Models + Data + Infrastructure + Agents + Applications + Governance.

Most people are focused on the model.

The real opportunities may be hiding in everything around it.

Save this AI ecosystem map. It’s worth revisiting as the industry evolves.

content:
Very interesting new paper from NVIDIA.

(bookmark it)

It takes a closer look at evaluating agent skills.

Enterprise teams are starting to leverage shared skill libraries, and the review gate is typically a scanner that checks structure, style, and security.

NVIDIA measured whether that gate predicts anything.

Across 145 real skills from internal and public catalogs, structural scan scores correlate with LLM-judge quality at a Spearman rho of 0.14.

ACES proposes Skill Lift instead.

In other words, run the same task twice under the same model, sandbox, workspace, and scorer, once with the skill loaded and once without. Then you measure the difference in what the agent completed.

They scored 947 paired cases from 58 production skills across four harnesses, normalizing trajectories into a shared Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, so results compare across harnesses.

They fins that the largest process-metric gains appear in skill execution, behavior check, and skill efficiency.

Paper: https://t.co/NDIO8yF3nr

Track more trending AI papers in our academy: https://t.co/1e8RZKs4uX

spending limits, whitelists, transaction policies, human approval, kill switches… could become a very important part of the agent stack.

that’s why i’m paying more attention to wallet + permission infrastructure, instead of only looking at AI agent tokens.

the more autonomous AI becomes, the more valuable the capital control layer behind it becomes.

content:
LOOPS VS GRAPHS: THE DISTINCTION THAT GETS YOU PROMOTED IN 2026

same ticket. two ways to resolve it. pick wrong and it burns your weekend

• loops
you set the frame. the agent owns the path
draft reply -> check vs policy -> resolved? -> no, loop again
best when you don't know the path yet

• graphs
you draw the path. the agent fills each node
read the ticket -> known issue? -> fix or investigate -> draft -> QA passes? -> review passes? -> send -> log
best when it's the same pipeline every day

what it looks like on disk:

📁 support-agent
┃
┣📁 Loop
┃ ┣📁 /goal.md
┃ ┣📁 /policy.md
┃ ┗📁 /retry.md
┃
┣📁 Graph
┃ ┣📁 /nodes.yml
┃ ┗📁 /edges.yml
┃
┣📁 Company Brain
┃ ┣📁 /tickets.md
┃ ┗📁 /product-docs.md
┃
┗📁 State
  ┗📁 /log.md

both shapes read from the same company brain. skip it and the agent relearns your business every run

start with a loop while the work is messy
freeze it into a graph once it stabilizes

slower to start, but you own the shape of it

// Applying Anthropic Primitives at Large Enterprises //

Frontier models collapsed the cost of writing custom code.

But they did not reduce the cost of reviewing and maintaining it.

Each bespoke solution drifts from the next. This means that there is a huge tax that goes into understanding them because this means reading their codebase from scratch.

The usual answers, an off the shelf product, a graph orchestration framework wired per use case, or a low code platform used as orchestrator, are custom every time and limited in scope.

This position paper argues for the harness paradigm instead. One coding agent harness runs unmodified as the backbone, with identical code across every deployment.

It builds on three recent findings. Harnesses suffice at the task level and outperform more elaborate architectures on enterprise work. Harness choice accounts for more variance in agent benchmark results than model choice does.

content:
There are two kinds of people in the AI era.

One says: “I’m not good at coding.”

The other opens Cursor + Claude Code, builds a rough first version, breaks a few things, fixes them, and keeps moving.

That gap is becoming more important than the skill gap itself.

AI does not magically make everyone a developer, designer, writer, researcher, or entrepreneur.

What it does is dramatically reduce the distance between “I have an idea” and “I built something.”

And that changes the game.

Can’t code? → Cursor + Claude Code

Can’t build an app? → Lovable + Bolt

Can’t design UI? → Figma AI + Uizard

Can’t edit videos? → Runway + CapCut AI

Can’t research fast enough? → Perplexity + Genspark

Can’t write well? → Claude + Jasper

Can’t build AI agents? → n8n + Flowise

Can’t automate repetitive work? → Zapier + Make

Can’t create presentations quickly? → Gamma + Canva AI

Can’t brainstorm? → ChatGPT + Gemini

Can’t learn fast enough? → NotebookLM + ChatGPT

Can’t grow on LinkedIn? → Taplio + AuthoredUp

Can’t build an online business? → Shopify Magic + Durable AI

The advantage is no longer knowing every tool.

The advantage is knowing which problem you are solving, which tool can remove the bottleneck, and how to connect those tools into a workflow.

So stop asking: “Which AI tool should I learn?”

Start asking: “What am I unable to do today that AI can help me do tomorrow?”

Then build. Test. Improve. Repeat.

AI will not replace effort.

But it is creating an enormous advantage for people who are willing to move before they feel completely ready.

7. Ask the AI to add those tokens into the Paper theme
8. Re-create one reference card using only tokens (quality check)
9. Refine tokens and add additional ones (muted/darker colors, 0 spacing, etc.)
10. Done!

content:
We built our own coding harness, just like Claude Code. (100% open-source)

A harness is the code wrapped around an LLM. The model only decides the next step, and the harness handles everything else, planning, tools, memory, and safety.

In simple words model acts as the brain and the harness provides the hands.

A coding harness is that same wrapper pointed at a codebase. It turns a plain text generator into something that reads files, edits code, runs tests, and fixes real bugs.

Here's everything that went into ours:

- the core agent loop
- file tools that double as external memory
- planning for long-running tasks
- subagents that work in their own context
- sandboxed execution in a throwaway VM
- human-in-the-loop approval
- persistent memory and checkpointing

The whole thing is built on CrewAI, a 100% open-source framework.

We also wrote an article on this. It covers everything that goes into building a coding harness, the agent loop, planning, subagents, sandboxing, memory, and checkpointing, built step by step.

The article is quoted below.

content:
Someone open-sourced an entire company that runs 24/7 on your laptop.

14 autonomous AI agents. One markdown file for memory. No vector DB.

Auto-Company is a multi-agent system where each role is modeled after a real expert. CEO thinks like Jeff Bezos. CTO like Werner Vogels. Inversion like Charlie Munger. Full-stack like DHH. Marketing like Seth Godin. Product design like Don Norman.

14 personas across strategy, product, engineering, business, and intel. Plus a shared arsenal of 30+ skills (deep research, security audit, financial modeling, SEO, etc.) any agent can load mid-cycle.

The interesting part is how it stays alive without going in circles.

Most multi-agent setups have two failure modes. Either they get stuck in endless discussion loops where every agent adds an opinion and nothing ships, or they need a complex vector database to carry context across sessions.

Auto-Company kills both.

Every cycle is an independent CLI call to Claude Code or Codex. The only cross-cycle state is a single markdown file called consensus md. Read at the start of a cycle, rewritten at the end. That's the baton.

No embeddings, no memory manager, no orchestration graph. Just a shared doc that the next cycle reads.

To prevent talking loops, it hardcodes a convergence flow:

- Cycle 1: brainstorm, rank top 3 ideas
- Cycle 2: pre-mortem, market check, unit economics, GO or NO-GO
- Cycle 3+: GO means build, deploy, ship. NO-GO means move on.

Pure discussion cycles are explicitly forbidden.

The daemon runs on launchd (mac) or systemd --user (WSL), auto-restarts on crash, and ships with circuit breakers, rate-limit backoff, and consensus rollback if a cycle doesn't produce valid output.

A local dashboard shows real-time cycle status, cost consumption, and agent activity.

And when you want to steer it, you don't restart anything. You just edit "Next Action" in consensus md. The next cycle picks up the new direction.

MIT licensed. Works with Claude Code or Codex CLI.

content:
The “7 Layers of AI” — and why understanding the difference matters 🤖

AI is often discussed as if it were one single technology.
It isn’t.

What we call Artificial Intelligence is really a progression of ideas built over decades — each layer adding new capabilities to the one before it.
1️⃣ Classical AI
The earliest systems relied on rules, logic, search and expert knowledge. Humans essentially told the machine what rules to follow.
2️⃣ Machine Learning
Instead of explicitly programming every decision, we started letting machines learn patterns from data.
3️⃣ Neural Networks
Networks of interconnected computational units made it possible to learn much richer representations from complex data.
4️⃣ Deep Learning
By stacking many neural-network layers, machines became remarkably good at vision, speech, language, recommendation and pattern recognition.
This is the technological foundation behind much of the AI revolution we have seen over the last decade.
5️⃣ Generative AI ✨
Now machines can generate text, images, audio, video and code.
Systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Midjourney have made this capability visible to hundreds of millions of people.
But generating impressive output should not automatically be confused with intelligence.
Fluency is not the same as understanding.
6️⃣ Agentic AI 🧠⚙️
This is where things become particularly interesting.
AI systems are increasingly able to:
• plan multi-step tasks
• use external tools
• search for information
• interact with software
• call APIs
• evaluate results
• take actions toward a goal
Instead of simply answering a question, an AI system can begin to do something.
This is arguably where much of the current frontier is moving.
And then there is…
7️⃣ AGI — Artificial General Intelligence
AGI would imply intelligence that can flexibly understand, learn and operate across a very broad range of tasks and environments.
We are not there yet.

Today's systems can be extraordinarily capable while still lacking many characteristics of robust human intelligence: grounded understanding, reliable reasoning, persistent world models, common sense and the ability to learn continually from real-world experience.
That distinction matters.

🚀 The biggest mistake in today's AI discussion is collapsing all these layers into one.
If we underestimate current AI, we miss enormous opportunities.
If we exaggerate it, we confuse impressive statistical learning with human-level intelligence.
The more productive question is not:
"Is AI intelligent?"
It is:
What capabilities does this system actually have, what are its limitations, and what technological breakthroughs are still required for the next layer?

AI is not magic.
It is a remarkable sequence of scientific and engineering advances — and the journey is far from finished.

content:
Watching devs slander “vibe coders” is so tiring.

Sure, if you really want to prove a vibe-coded app is “bad,” you can run load tests until it blows past its DB connection limits, inject network chaos to expose missing circuit breakers, run 48-hour soak tests to uncover memory leaks, or audit a monolith under 50k users for unindexed queries, N+1s, row locks, thread starvation, and broken cache invalidation.

And after all that, you might discover something uncomfortable: 95% of software doesn’t need any of it.

Most people vibe coding aren’t trying to build the next Google. They’re turning an idea into functional software for 50 users, solving a problem, learning, or just having fun.

Software engineering is much deeper than pulling out enterprise-scale benchmarks to dunk on something someone built on the internet.

There’s distributed systems, performance engineering, databases, compilers, networking, concurrency, system design, and a thousand genuinely hard problems to master.

You don’t need to fight vibe coders to prove you’re an engineer.

Let people build. Then go build something hard yourself.

SpaceXAI will deploy NVIDIA Vera CPUs to accelerate its next generat
content:
BREAKING: NVIDIA just published a new blog post detailing how SpaceXAI will use Vera CPUs to scale agentic AI from Earth to orbit:

SpaceXAI will deploy NVIDIA Vera CPUs to accelerate its next generation of agentic AI applications, bringing the first CPU built for AI agents to one of the world’s most ambitious AI deployments.

Agentic AI applications increasingly rely on CPUs to orchestrate tools, execute code, process data and run simulations between model calls. SpaceXAI will use Vera to accelerate these application workloads, helping AI agents act faster while keeping GPUs fed and fully utilized.

SpaceXAI plans to expand its AI infrastructure behind Grok on NVIDIA Vera Rubin, while extending an optimized Vera Rubin NVL72 into space with its first-generation Starmind satellite.

“Agentic AI requires a new kind of computing system — one built not only to generate answers, but to take action,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Vera gives AI agents the CPU performance to act in real time — executing code, processing data and coordinating complex tasks. SpaceXAI is taking this architecture from massive AI factories to the next frontier of computing in orbit.”

“Vera gives us the CPU performance and memory bandwidth to run enormous amounts of orchestration, code and data processing while keeping GPUs doing what they do best,” said Mike Nicolls, president of SpaceXAI. “That means higher-performance AI agents and more useful work from every watt of compute.”

VIDIA Vera — The CPU for Agents
NVIDIA Vera is the first CPU built for AI agents, designed to accelerate the CPU-intensive work that surrounds model inference — from tool use and code execution to data processing, orchestration and simulation.

Vera features 88 NVIDIA-designed Olympus cores, NVIDIA Spatial Multithreading technology and high-bandwidth LPDDR5X memory, delivering up to 1.2TB/s of bandwidth. Vera enables up to 1.8x faster task completion compared with x86 CPUs across workloads including agentic AI, reinforcement learning and data processing.

SpaceXAI Scales AI Infrastructure With NVIDIA Vera Rubin
At massive scale, AI infrastructure must support demanding training, reasoning and inference workloads while maximizing performance, power efficiency and utilization. NVIDIA Vera Rubin is codesigned across compute, networking and software to optimize the AI factory as a whole.

The platform brings together NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA NVLink™ interconnect technology, NVIDIA Spectrum-X™ Ethernet networking, NVIDIA BlueField® data processing and NVIDIA software in an integrated architecture designed to deliver high performance and energy efficiency at scale while driving down cost per token.
As SpaceXAI expands toward gigawatts of computing capacity, Vera Rubin provides a common architecture to efficiently scale its next generation of AI factories — a foundation SpaceXAI plans to take beyond terrestrial data centers and into orbital computing.

NVIDIA Accelerated Computing, From Earth to Orbit
SpaceXAI’s work with NVIDIA is moving beyond AI factories on Earth.

SpaceXAI is developing AI computing infrastructure for orbit, where power, thermal management, bandwidth, reliability and physical integration impose dramatically different constraints from conventional data centers.

SpaceXAI’s planned first-generation Starmind AI satellite will be based on the optimized NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, extending the same accelerated computing architecture powering next-generation AI factories on Earth into space.
NVIDIA and SpaceXAI are working to adapt that foundation to the requirements of orbital computing while preserving a common NVIDIA architecture and software ecosystem.

This delivers one computing foundation across a wide range of environments: Vera CPUs accelerating increasingly sophisticated AI agents, Vera Rubin powering the AI infrastructure behind Grok and gigawatt-scale AI factories on Earth, and NVIDIA accelerated computing extending into orbital AI infrastructure.

Today we release Pipette, a model evaluation suite for on-device intelligence, in partnership with @ArtificialAnlys 

Most benchmarking platforms are optimized to measure core capabilities and speed profile of foundation models served in the cloud. Pipette gives the field a common, reproducible way to measure the quality, speed, latency, and memory use of AI models on devices such as phones, laptops, PCs, AI boxes, and embedded hardware.

> Pipette is open source
> In Pipette, models get compated as model + quantization + runtime + device from one interface.
> It comes with a warehouse of verified benchmark results, currently with 10k+ results across 35 model classes, 7 quants, llama.cpp runtimes, and 4 devices.
> Pipette is a dynamic platform, allowing new contributions from day one, adding new devices, runtimes, model families, and quantization levels.

title: Brandon Spangler did five years in the Marine Corps. He broke his neck, crushed his lower back, and walked out with a VA prescription that turned into eight years of addiction. The last stretch was he
content:
Brandon Spangler did five years in the Marine Corps. He broke his neck, crushed his lower back, and walked out with a VA prescription that turned into eight years of addiction. The last stretch was heroin. He got sober in 2013, started college from zero, and is now a licensed clinical social worker with his own practice for cops and veterans in northwest Montana. Travis Gribble spent 24 years in law enforcement, 16 on SWAT, and retired out of Mesa PD in 2022. He now works for the Boulder Crest Foundation.

He walks through the jump from pharmacy to street, detoxing cold turkey three times, and a month and a half living out of a truck in the Blue Mountains waiting on a bed.

Both of them are done with PTSD as an identity. Why the D on the end matters. Why most people process trauma without a diagnosis. What happens when a man grabs hold of being called broken.

Also in here: moral injury, the 400 to 600 traumatic calls a cop absorbs over a career, why the average officer dies seven years after retiring, and the retainer model that put a therapist inside a sheriff's office.

title: The biggest problem with AI today is not always the intelligence but the lack of ownership around the conversations that create that intelligence. Every question, preference, decision, and piece of co
content:
The biggest problem with AI today is not always the intelligence but the lack of ownership around the conversations that create that intelligence. Every question, preference, decision, and piece of context can become part of a centralized system that users have very little control over. A sovereign AI in @TheARCTERMINAL approach changes this by making privacy and ownership part of the architecture instead of treating them as optional features. The idea of placing an intermediary between the user and the AI can create stronger separation while still allowing the system to deliver useful responses. This becomes especially important as people use AI for increasingly personal, financial, and professional conversations. The future of AI should not only be about smarter models but also about giving users stronger control over the information they generate.

Persistent memory is another area where AI can become significantly more useful when it is designed around user ownership. Most AI experiences can remember context only within certain limits or depend heavily on centralized systems to store conversation history. A sovereign memory layer could allow users to carry their context across conversations without giving a platform unlimited control over that information. This means AI can become more personalized while the underlying data remains under stronger user control. The interesting part is that privacy and personalization do not necessarily have to compete with each other. If the architecture is designed correctly, users can have an AI that understands their history without feeling like their entire digital identity is sitting openly inside someone else's database.

PATHOS introduces another interesting direction because understanding a user is not only about remembering individual messages. Human communication contains patterns involving mood, momentum, habits, priorities, and changes in behavior over time. A lightweight model that focuses on these patterns could make AI interactions feel more continuous without requiring a massive model to analyze everything from scratch. Instead of simply remembering what someone said, the system can potentially understand how the conversation has evolved. This could make AI feel less like a collection of disconnected chats and more like a persistent relationship with context. The important distinction is that useful memory should help the user while still respecting boundaries around what should and should not be remembered.

Crypto adds another layer to this vision because ownership can extend beyond conversation history into identity, assets, and financial activity. An AI system that can interact with onchain portfolios while keeping keys locally controlled could become more than a chatbot. It could become a personal interface for managing information, digital assets, and autonomous workflows without requiring users to surrender complete control to a centralized platform. This is where decentralized AI becomes interesting because blockchain can provide ownership and settlement while AI provides intelligence and automation. Local key custody is particularly important because convenience should not require giving a third party complete authority over valuable assets. The combination of private memory, autonomous intelligence, and user controlled assets could become a powerful foundation for the next generation of AI applications.

The bigger idea is that AI should evolve from a service people temporarily use into infrastructure that people actually own and control. Persistent memory in @TheARCTERMINAL can make AI more useful, privacy architecture can make it more trustworthy, and crypto can provide the ownership layer needed for digital assets and identity. Together, these technologies create a vision where the AI remembers what matters without exposing everything to a centralized platform. That is a very different model from simply making larger models and collecting more user data. The strongest AI systems of the future may be the ones that understand users deeply while giving those users more control over how that understanding is created and stored. Sovereign AI is ultimately about making intelligence personal without making privacy the price of personalization.

content:
I love bones (Part 2). This article reveals how fascinating and complicated bone biology and physiology are. It’s a bit long… but it goes deep.

I’ve been an orthopedic surgeon for 30 years. I have fixed hundreds of fractures. I have operated on spines, hips, and wrists weakened by osteoporosis. And in my experience, almost nobody understands what a bone actually is, its role in our overall health, or why it fails.

Most people think of bone the way they think of the steel frame of a building. Static and structural... meaning it's either intact or broken.

This conceptual model is wrong, and understanding why is the foundation for protecting yourself against osteoporosis.  1 in 3 women and 1 in 5 men will develop osteoporosis. Women will spend more time in the hospital for osteoporosis-related fractures than for breast cancer and heart disease combined. You need to know how your bones work and how to build them. 

Your skeleton is not a fixed structure. It's living tissue that is constantly being renewed. Right now, specialized cells are dissolving small sections of your bone, while other cells are rebuilding them. This process never stops. It runs continuously from birth until death. And when it falls out of balance — for any of several well-understood reasons — bone loss begins. 
Let’s get into this…

Unlike digital AI, robotics lacks abundant data and low-cost distribution, making the path from demo to
content:
Physical AI is emerging as a ~$40T opportunity, nearly 7x the estimated market for digital AI.

Unlike digital AI, robotics lacks abundant data and low-cost distribution, making the path from demo to business harder.

So which path can turn physical intelligence into a scalable business?

—
● Physical AI: From Demos to Deployment
Robots can already drive, pick and pack, fold laundry, and operate in factories and data centers. Turning these demos into reliable commercial systems remains the challenge.

Physical AI extends beyond cognitive work into manufacturing, logistics, construction, and infrastructure.

—
● The Physical AI Data Flywheel
Deploy -> collect real-world data -> learn from failures -> improve models -> automate more tasks -> deploy again.

The bottleneck is high-quality physical data. Robotics lacks the abundant, transferable training data that powered digital AI.

Teleoperation captures difficult edge cases, while customer deployments generate the data needed to improve reliability.

—
● Why Physical AI Won’t Have a ChatGPT Moment
Software scales almost instantly. Robots require:
• Manufacturing and shipping
• Installation and workflow integration
• Maintenance and repairs

That makes robotics feedback loops take years instead of weeks.

Physical AI will likely progress task-by-task and vertical-by-vertical, giving deployment-first companies time to build proprietary data and customer relationships.

—
● Three Paths to Physical AI
Three strategies are emerging, each attacking the same reliability problem from a different direction:
• Foundation model / model-first: Build general-purpose intelligence first, then scale across robots and tasks.

• Deployment-first: Deploy robots into real businesses and use them to generate proprietary data.

• Full-stack: Own the model, hardware, deployment, and data loop end-to-end.

—
The strongest Physical AI companies may not be the ones with the best demos, but those building the fastest deployment and data flywheels.

As models improve, proprietary data and deep customer integration could become the industry's strongest moats.

The advantage will come from closing the loop between deployment, data, reliability, and autonomy faster than competitors.

content:
GPT Image 2 Prompt Share

Theme Based Collage Template

A flexible collage prompt for turning any theme into a series of connected visual moments. Change the parameters as you wish. Example values in the alts.

Prompt:
THEME = enter theme
STYLE = enter the style you want
PALETTE = enter the color palette
ASPECT RATIO = enter the aspect ratio you want

DO:
  Create an artistic multi-scene collage built entirely around THEME.
  Derive subjects, environments, objects, characters and visual events naturally from THEME.
  Derive the emotional tone, atmosphere and energy naturally from THEME.
  Use people, animals, objects, landscapes, architecture, abstract forms or any combination of them when they meaningfully support THEME.
  Treat each scene as a distinct emotional or conceptual fragment from the same world.
  Build the composition like an expressive editorial art spread rather than a storyboard or regular panel grid.
  Freely vary the number, scale, proportions and placement of scenes.
  Combine large dominant images with narrow vertical fragments, wide horizontal crops, small detail scenes and partially cropped compositions.
  Stagger scene edges and shift their alignments to create an irregular visual rhythm.
  Let some scenes extend fully to the canvas edge while others terminate against neighboring imagery.
  Use occasional L-shaped, stepped or offset arrangements created naturally by neighboring scene proportions.
  Avoid repeating the same rectangle size or alignment across the composition.
  Keep scenes visually separate without visible frames or empty gaps between them.
  Let neighboring scenes meet through irregular crop relationships while keeping their environments independent.
  Do not blend separate locations into one continuous environment.
  Keep the main subjects of each scene visually contained within that scene.
  Use architecture, large color fields and negative space to shape the overall composition.
  Connect neighboring scenes through color relationships, visual rhythm and thematic echoes rather than physically merging their content.
  Choose environments and situations specifically suited to THEME.
  Include occasional intimate fragments such as hands, objects, windows, silhouettes, architectural details or empty spaces when they strengthen THEME.
  Give each scene a different visual scale, point of view and conceptual focus.
  Use expressive lighting, shape, perspective and negative space according to STYLE.
  Vary the emphasis of PALETTE from scene to scene while preserving overall harmony.
  Maintain consistency whenever subjects, characters, objects or locations recur.
  Keep the final composition visually clean, sophisticated and intentionally irregular.

CAMERA: varied editorial framing, environmental wides, cropped medium views, isolated details, unusual negative-space compositions, overhead fragments and off-center perspectives chosen according to THEME

RULES:
  Use STYLE as the authority for medium, linework, texture, shading, shape design and overall rendering language.
  Use PALETTE as the dominant color system across the image.
  Let THEME determine subjects, setting, mood, symbolism and visual narrative.
  Every scene must explore a different facet of THEME.
  The composition must feel assembled, layered and rhythmically irregular rather than divided into uniform boxes.
  Keep individual scenes independently readable while allowing their shapes and proportions to interact compositionally.
  Use asymmetry, scale contrast, staggered alignment and varied cropping to create the collage structure.
  Do not use visible panel outlines.
  Render every surface freshly, with continuous natural texture flow.
  Keep grain fine, stochastic, and evenly distributed across the frame.
  Give each repeated element its own unique micro-variation.
  Keep flat areas smooth with clean, unbroken tonal gradients.
  Resolve fine detail crisply at native resolution, as a first-generation render.

NO: rigid grid, equal-sized panels, repeated rectangular boxes, visible panel borders, white gutters, margins, outer padding, blended environments, fused scenes, characters spanning multiple scenes, conventional comic-page layout, speech bubbles, captions, text, logos, watermarks

title:
SenseNova-Vision: Vision as Unified Multimodal Generation
https://t.co/Y97zOo56JL
SenseNova-Vision formulate computer vision as unified multimodal generation, where heterogeneous visual tasks are expr
content:
SenseNova-Vision: Vision as Unified Multimodal Generation
https://t.co/Y97zOo56JL
SenseNova-Vision formulate computer vision as unified multimodal generation, where heterogeneous visual tasks are expressed through the native text and image generation spaces of a unified multimodal model (UMM). Natural-language instructions and optional visual prompts specify the task, target regions or views, output schema, and decoding convention, while the model responds through native text, image, or mixed text-image generation.

Text generation expresses symbolic visual records such as categories, boxes, points, OCR strings, keypoints, and camera parameters. Image generation handles dense spatial targets such as segmentation masks, depth maps, surface normals, and multi-view point maps. Mixed responses support compositional tasks that combine symbolic and dense outputs. This shared formulation lets one model cover structured visual understanding, dense geometric prediction, segmentation, and multi-view visual geometry while keeping outputs decodable for standard benchmarks.

To enable large-scale training, we convert heterogeneous computer-vision annotations into instruction-response examples and construct the SenseNova-Vision Corpus, spanning decodable text, image, and mixed text-image targets. Starting from an off-the-shelf pretrained UMM, SenseNova-Vision is trained primarily on this corpus, with auxiliary multimodal data used to preserve general understanding and generation capability, and requires no task-specific prediction heads, decoders, or architectural branches.

------

The cost of creating or modifying an application will now depend on:

- Application complexity;
- AI resources required;
- Processing workload needed for creation or updates.

Pi stated that the pricing is designed to reflect the actual service cost rather than adding additional profit margins.

Applications that demonstrate:

✅ Real independent users;
✅ Strong engagement;
✅ Meaningful contribution to the Pi ecosystem;

This creates a new ecosystem principle:

Useful applications → More users → More support

Unlimited creation → Many inactive applications.

The first stage focused on encouraging Pioneer creativity and experimentation.

The next stage focuses on:

- Quality;
- Utility;
- Sustainability;
- Real-world adoption.

Pi is moving from:

"Create more apps"

"Build valuable applications."

AI application platforms often face challenges:

- Thousands of experimental apps;
- Low user activity;
- High infrastructure costs.

- Pi Commerce;

- AI tools;
- Community services.

Developers will need to focus more on:

- User experience;
- Practical value;
- User retention;
- Pi Payment integration;

Sustainable business models.

The ecosystem is moving from:

"Build an App"

toward:
"Build a Real Utility Ecosystem."

------

🔗 Connection With Pi Mainnet Strategy

This update aligns with Pi’s broader ecosystem development:

- Pi App Studio has continued improving its capabilities, including persistent storage features that allow apps to save and retrieve user-specific data.
- Pi is building toward applications that can operate with real utility rather than simple demonstrations.

The combination of:

Pi App Studio + Persistent Storage + Pi Payments + Mainnet Infrastructure

creates the foundation for a stronger Web3 application ecosystem.

------

🌎 GCV Commerce Perspective

For the GCV ecosystem, this update highlights the importance of applications that support:

- Merchants;
- Marketplaces;
- Payments;
- Supply chains;
- AI commerce;
- Business management.

The future value of an application will come from:

✅ Real users

Applications that create practical value will become key components of the Pi economy.

------

August 24, 2026 marks an important transition for Pi App Studio:
From encouraging unlimited creation → to supporting high-quality, valuable applications.
The message is clear:
The growth of the Pi ecosystem will not be measured only by the number of applications created, but by the real value those applications bring to millions of Pioneers.
Pi App Studio continues moving toward the vision of a decentralized application economy powered by AI, utility, and real-world adoption.

content:
GM FAM 🫳

Why Shipping Makes RWA More Interesting

☞ The more I look at @EthraShip the more I think the real opportunity isn’t simply putting ships onchain.

It’s building a better financial and information layer around an industry that already works.

Commercial shipping has something many RWA narratives are missing: constant real-world demand.

☞ Dry bulk vessels move essential commodities across global markets, creating economic activity regardless of whether crypto is having a good week or a bad one.

That creates an interesting foundation for Web3.

Instead of starting with:

What can we do with this token?

The better question becomes:

What problems already exist in this industry that blockchain can actually improve?

And there are plenty:

→ Better visibility into vessel activity
→ More structured access to maritime opportunities
→ Transparent onchain participation
→ Better coordination between capital and real assets
→ Reliable data around physical operations

This is where I think EthraShip has an interesting direction.

The physical business doesn’t need blockchain to exist.

The ships don’t need a token to move cargo.

The industry already has operators, contracts, assets, revenue and established market demand.

Blockchain can instead become the coordination and access layer sitting around that existing economy.

That’s a much more convincing RWA thesis to me.

Because the strongest projects won’t be the ones that simply attach a token to something physical.

They’ll be the ones that understand the underlying industry first, then carefully introduce technology where it actually adds value.

Real industry first.
Infrastructure second.
Tokenization where it makes sense.

That’s the kind of RWA model I’m watching closely.

The ships keep moving.

The question is how much better the financial and information rails around them can become.

content:
Astra may have quietly revealed where AGI arrives first.

look at the public signals from Astra: mathematical arguments that end in Lean certificates, agentic coding, and cyber evaluations requiring functional exploits. they seem unrelated. each gives the model a judge that fluent language cannot fool.

a proof checks. a program passes its tests. an exploit works against the target. failure is cheap and a correct artifact is unambiguous. with tools, memory and enough attempts, errors can become branches in a search.

this may explain why the sharpest capability jumps keep appearing in technical fields. writing, taste, management and politics have fuzzy feedback. there is no compiler for good judgment. mathematics, software, cyber, chip design and parts of biology can be surrounded by tests that score attempt after attempt.

OpenAI’s own scientific-computing report says researchers are already moving from implementation toward “verification and orchestration”: defining what to build, deciding how correctness will be measured and auditing the result.

the scarce skill in the Astra era may be designing the verifier, turning an important goal into a test the model cannot game.

AGI may arrive unevenly. some fields could feel post-human while meetings, management and politics remain painfully human.

the next trillion-dollar question: what valuable work can be converted into a test that cannot be faked?

title:
Talk Condensed Summary of @pduan , Head of Tesla’s FSD,  present at CVPR 2026 workshop 

@Tesla completely rewrote autonomous driving from modular assembly into a single video foundation model that pr
content:
Talk Condensed Summary of @pduan , Head of Tesla’s FSD,  present at CVPR 2026 workshop 

@Tesla completely rewrote autonomous driving from modular assembly into a single video foundation model that predicts the next action. It is Video in, Action out, following the same methodology as training GPT.

Modular approaches fail because interface errors accumulate, the long tail cannot be exhaustively enumerated, and they go against the Bitter Lesson. End-to-end enables homogeneous compute and deterministic latency.

The core difficulty is the curse of dimensionality. The input consists of massive tokens from 8 high-resolution cameras, while the output is essentially only two degrees of freedom: steering and acceleration. The model easily learns shortcuts and forms spurious correlations, for example treating background green as a signal to go straight.

The solution is multi-task co-training with proxy tasks. Tesla demoted previous tasks such as segmentation, detection, depth, 3D occupancy, OCR, and human mesh (about 16 categories) into auxiliary signals used only during training. These tasks supply dense gradients, force the model to build correct representations, and inject true causality. At deployment the system outputs only actions. Proxy task metrics only need to be healthy enough. The sole real metric is driving performance.

The data engine is the moat. Roughly 7 million vehicles generate about 500 years of driving time daily. A typical training set exceeds 120 years and hundreds of petabytes. Tesla uses disagreement mining (segments where the model and human drivers differ) for active learning, and applies offline auto-labeling with cloud teacher models to generate 3D ground truth. Internet video and Optimus data are also incorporated to improve generalization, such as recognizing a chair on the highway.

For safety, imitation learning teaches how humans usually drive, while reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards teaches what must never be done. Collision is a perfect verifiable signal. At deployment there is no rule-based safety layer. The system relies entirely on the model itself.

On compute, by June 2026 Tesla reached approximately 280,000 H100 equivalents, approaching 300,000, while keeping a small team with high GPU resources per engineer.

In summary, the old modular tasks did not die. They simply changed from the system skeleton into training scaffolding. The claim that end-to-end equals a black box is a misunderstanding. Intermediate representations exist in large quantities. They are simply no longer exported on the vehicle.

content:
Good Morning 

A lot of Web3 projects are building toward the same thing: making the systems around us more intelligent, verifiable, and valuable.

Most health apps still work like reports.
They collect your data, show you a score, and leave the decisions to you.

@sleepagotchi is pushing into something different: agentic AI for wellness.

Instead of stopping at the dashboard, the system is being built to turn personal sleep and recovery data into actual guidance and actions.

Sleep Coach already lets you ask questions grounded in your own patterns, not population averages.

Wearables solved data collection.
The next layer is intelligence that knows what to do with it.

That shift is still early, but the direction is clear.

Contribution in Web3 is still mostly temporary.

You show up for a campaign, perform, collect, and the signal mostly resets.

@NucleusCodes is trying to make reputation travel.

Season 3 is live, with real rewards tied to ranking.

The deeper idea is more important than any single season: distribution based on accumulated signal instead of pure short-term noise.

When platforms can read existing reputation, they waste less energy on fake activity and reward people who stay consistent.

That model is still rare.
It is also the one that compounds.

Most RWA projects start with a token and a story.

@EthraShip started with ships.

Real vessels.
Years of operating experience.
Market cycles already lived through.

Now they are building the onchain participation and verification layers on top of that foundation Ethra Harbor for access, Sea Verity for maritime intelligence.

Aging fleets, limited new supply, and shifting trade dynamics make the underlying market interesting on its own.

The difference is that this is not theoretical exposure to shipping.

It is an attempt to open a real operating business to broader participation.

Proof still matters more than narrative here.

Big communities create reach.
They also create noise.

@IronAllies_ is optimizing for the opposite.

A gated network where contribution is the currency.

You earn $IRON by creating value for other members, then spend it on access, visibility, and opportunities.

Iron Lords sit at the top as a scarce VIP layer with stronger alignment.

The design is simple and strict:

High-signal people helping each other grow, with an internal economy that makes that behavior profitable.

In a market full of temporary attention, selective networks with real incentives are becoming more interesting.

Most people still talk about quantum computing like it is pure science fiction.

@quipnetwork is treating it as two practical problems:

1.Useful quantum and high.performance compute should be accessible through an open network.

2.Existing wallets and contracts need protection before quantum attacks become realistic.

The compute layer turns work into something economically useful instead of pure hash grinding.

The asset layer lets people add post-quantum protection to systems they already use, without waiting for a full migration.

One side is about future capability.
The other is about not being late to a known risk.

That dual approach is still under-discussed.

Different problems.
Different industries.
But one common direction:

Less blind trust.
More intelligence.
More verifiable value.
More systems that actually reward meaningful participation.

That is the direction I find most interesting.

title:
The next big question in AI isn’t just “How intelligent is the agent?”

It’s “Who stands behind it?”

AI agents are moving toward a future where they can negotiate agreements, execute payments, manage
content:
The next big question in AI isn’t just “How intelligent is the agent?”

It’s “Who stands behind it?”

AI agents are moving toward a future where they can negotiate agreements, execute payments, manage assets, interact with smart contracts, and operate across digital economies with minimal human intervention.

The possibilities are huge. But greater autonomy also creates a bigger need for accountability.

If an agent makes a costly mistake, moves funds incorrectly, breaks a rule, or acts maliciously, who takes responsibility?

This is where @Concordium’s identity infrastructure becomes particularly interesting.

Rather than treating identity and compliance as something added later, Concordium is working to make them part of the underlying infrastructure creating a verifiable connection between an autonomous agent and the human or organisation behind it.

The model becomes simple:

Human → Verified Identity → AI Agent → On-chain Action

The agent can operate autonomously, while the ecosystem still has a way to establish who is responsible for its actions.

As AI evolves from generating information to making decisions and moving real value, that distinction could become critical.

The future may not be about anonymous agents operating without accountability.

It could be about agents that can prove who they represent, what they’re authorised to do, and who stands behind their actions.

AI gives agents the ability to act.
Blockchain provides the infrastructure to execute.
Identity provides the foundation for trust.

That’s why I’m watching @Concordium closely as the agentic economy continues to take shape.

Is funny how for years one of the biggest criticisms of Cardano was its eUTXO model. It was “too slow,” “too complicated,” and supposedly inferior to Ethereum’s architec
content:
CRYPTO COMMUNITY PLEASE READ!

Is funny how for years one of the biggest criticisms of Cardano was its eUTXO model. It was “too slow,” “too complicated,” and supposedly inferior to Ethereum’s architecture.

Now we have a proposal called “Native UTXOs on Ethereum.”

Corporations, companies, protocols, governments: pay attention. Blockchain architecture matters far more than most people realize.

Ethereum is now exploring UTXO-like properties because there are real advantages in state management, efficiency, and transaction design. Meanwhile, Cardano has been built around eUTXO from the beginning.

That’s the ironic part. Many of the things people used to criticize Cardano for came directly from its obsession with security, determinism, and building the foundation correctly first.

We’ve heard “Cardano is slow” for years. Sure, Cardano historically sacrificed some speed in favor of security and a more rigorous design. But that part is evolving too. Hydra is already here, and Leios is being developed to significantly increase network throughput.

Maybe Cardano was never as far behind as people thought.

Maybe it was simply building years earlier what others are now starting to realize they want.

author: GaryMarcus

title:
There is a crisis among men that I refuse to stay silent on.

Every day, men are let down. Men work, build businesses, raise families, buy homes and build lives, often through years of sacrifice, only
content:
There is a crisis among men that I refuse to stay silent on.

Every day, men are let down. Men work, build businesses, raise families, buy homes and build lives, often through years of sacrifice, only to find that what they have built can be taken from them, their character destroyed and their reputation ruined with frightening ease.

Men know this. Many are terrified. Terrified of approaching women. Terrified of entering relationships. Terrified that after years of building a life, everything can be turned against them. Terrified of being manipulated, financially destroyed, separated from their children, dragged through the courts or treated as guilty before the facts are established.

False allegations matter because they do not just destroy innocent men. They diminish the horrors experienced by genuine victims of rape, sexual assault and abuse by making it harder to distinguish truth from manipulation. We must be able to defend genuine victims while also defending innocent men.

The problem goes deeper than relationships. The state, courts, education system, government, public sector, private sector and popular culture have spent years telling men what they are doing wrong, what they are allowed to say and how masculine they are allowed to be. Feminism, particularly its most hostile forms, has contributed to a culture in which masculinity is treated as something that needs to be corrected rather than something that needs to be disciplined and directed.

Men are not asking for special treatment. They are asking for respect.

A man can endure an extraordinary amount of hardship when he knows he is respected, when he has purpose, responsibility and knows his contribution matters. Love matters. Warmth matters. Family matters. But respect comes above all else.

Too many men are mocked, humiliated, spoken down to and treated as disposable. The moment they raise their heads above the parapet, society comes down on them. Say the wrong thing and you are a misogynist. Stand up for yourself and you are toxic. Be masculine and you are dangerous. Be proud of being an Englishman and you can be told your very identity is oppressive. Make one mistake and you can be branded for life.

I do not accept it. And I am going to speak about it more.

I have a strong male following, and every day young British men message me or come up to me telling me they are grateful to have someone who speaks openly about these things. I am genuinely humbled by that responsibility.

Because I know what struggle looks like. I have experienced attacks I could never have predicted so early on in my life, physically and mentally; I don't talk about it because it is my private life. I have been in relationships and dynamics that disrupted me, tormented me and tortured me mentally for months at a time. I have struggled financially. I have built myself out of debt and homelessness. I have had to build parts of my life from scratch. I am still going through struggle today.

But I do not resent the struggle. I embrace it. I enjoy the pain. I enjoy the suffering. I enjoy the process of becoming stronger through it.

My mentality had to be built from scratch, but I also inherited something enormously valuable from my father: a foundation, a sense of responsibility and examples of what strength looks like.

Not every young man has that.

Some grow up without a father. Some grow up without a strong male role model. Some have nobody teaching them what masculinity should actually mean, instead they are constantly beaten down. Society removes every positive model of masculinity, gives young men nothing meaningful to replace it with, and then wonders why they become angry, isolated, nihilistic or misguided.

I don't believe in therapy. I don't believe in seeking professional help. I don't believe antidepressants or anti-anxiety medication - we do not need to medicate the struggle of man but respect it.

Rebuilding men cannot simply mean medicating their pain, endlessly analysing their emotions or telling them to open up more. We need to tell men something else: You are strong. You have responsibilities. You have a duty. You are capable. You are needed. You are responsible for what you do with your life.

Men need purpose. They need responsibility. They need brotherhood. They need fathers and role models. They need something worth sacrificing for. They need people who believe in them. And they need respect.

Men have a duty to their country, their families, their loved ones, their communities and the people who depend upon them. There is no permanent day off from that duty. There will be days when you are exhausted, hurt and have nothing left. You still get up. You still do what needs to be done, because you have chosen something greater than yourself.

Ultimately, I want to leave a mark on this world. One day I will die. So will every man reading this. The question is what we will have built before we go.

That should be the ambition for men. Not endless pleasure. Not victimhood. Not resentment. Build something. Protect something. Create something. Leave something behind.

Our ancestors understood this. Men before us went through wars, bloodshed, poverty, hardship, loss and unimaginable suffering. They fought. They worked. They built families, communities and nations. They did what duty demanded.

We are the beneficiaries of their sacrifice. We have a responsibility to the generation that comes after us.

Men drive change. Men have historically driven revolutions, built institutions, explored the unknown, fought wars and undertaken enormous projects that transformed civilisation. That does not mean women do not contribute enormously. It means men have a particular capacity for sacrifice, risk and responsibility that society should not be ashamed of cultivating.

We should not be emasculating men. We should be developing them.

We should not teach boys to hate masculinity. We should teach them to master it and have self control.

That is the message young men need.

I am not saying men are always right. I am not saying women are always wrong. I am not saying genuine victims should not be heard. I am saying innocent men deserve protection too. Good men deserve respect. Hard-working men deserve dignity. Fathers deserve recognition. Boys deserve role models.

People will read this and call it misogynistic, sexist or toxic masculinity.

I genuinely do not care and never have done.

I care about what I know to be true.

I know men matter. I know young men need direction. I know boys need strong role models. I know responsibility creates character. I know respect gives men a reason to keep building.

And I know that a society that continually tears down its men should not be surprised when its men stop believing that society is worth building.

So to the young men reading this: do not become bitter. Do not become weak. Do not become cruel. Do not allow a bad relationship, a bad institution, a false accusation or a cruel person to define you.

Build yourself. Get stronger. Take responsibility. Establish a brotherhood. Find good women. Build a family if that is what you want. Build a business. Build a home. Build a community. Serve your country. Protect the people you love. Seek help when you need it. Stand back up when you fall. Go to church.

Leave the world better than you found it.

Men do not need to be told that they are powerless.

They need to know that they are capable.

They need purpose, responsibility, discipline, brotherhood and a wife who loves & respects them.

Happy Sunday.

content:
🚨 INDIA: The truth behind the video circulating online.

A 19-year-old Indian man reportedly argued with his family after demanding a new iPhone. He climbed to the top of a mountain, stood near the edge and threatened to take his own life.

title:
Let’s take a step back. And east.

Augustus built Western civilization’s first institutional foundation. Charlemagne rebuilt it from the ruins. But before either of them, there was a Macedonian king w
content:
Let’s take a step back. And east.

Augustus built Western civilization’s first institutional foundation. Charlemagne rebuilt it from the ruins. But before either of them, there was a Macedonian king who, in thirteen years, spread the civilization that would become the West’s foundation across the entire known world. He did not build the West. He made the West possible. He was thirty-two when he died.

1. He was Aristotle’s student – the most consequential teacher-student relationship in history. For three years, before he became king, Alexander sat with Aristotle and was taught philosophy, science, and above all Homer. He kept the Iliad under his pillow alongside a dagger. He considered Achilles his model. The man who conquered the known world was formed by the philosopher who invented the method of reasoning from evidence that became the foundation of Western thought.

2. The military genius was unprecedented. He inherited a kingdom, crossed into Asia at twenty-two, and never lost a battle in thirteen years. Persia — the greatest empire the world had seen — fell in three years. Egypt, Mesopotamia, Central Asia, the Punjab – all conquered in a campaign covering thirty thousand kilometers on foot and horseback. Napoleon studied him. Wellington studied him. Every serious military commander for two millennia studied him.

3. But the military conquest is not the point. The civilizational gift is. Alexander didn’t just conquer – he planted. Over twenty cities named Alexandria – from Egypt to the edges of India, each one a center of Greek language, culture, and philosophy planted in conquered soil. He was building a network of civilization, not just an empire. He turned Greek culture from the inheritance of one people into the common language of an entire civilization, creating the first truly international language of intellectual exchange. The New Testament would be written in Greek three centuries after his death. The philosophical vocabulary that shaped early Christianity was Greek because Alexander had made Greek the language of the educated world from Egypt to India.

4. His most radical vision was synthesis. He adopted Persian dress and customs. He married into Persian royalty. He incorporated Persian nobles into his administration. He was creating something new – Greek rationalism fused with Eastern depth. His generals resisted. After his death they divided the empire. But the Hellenistic world that resulted was the most intellectually fertile environment in human history before the Renaissance.

5. Alexandria — founded when he was twenty-five — became the greatest city of the ancient world. The Library: the first systematic attempt to collect all human knowledge. The Museum: the first research institution in history. The confluence of Greek, Egyptian, Jewish, and Persian intellectual traditions that produced Euclid, Eratosthenes, and the Septuagint — the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible that shaped the theological vocabulary of Christianity.

6. Without Alexander, no West as we know it. Without Hellenization, no philosophical vocabulary for Christianity. Without that vocabulary, no Church Fathers, no medieval theology, no Aquinas, no scientific revolution. The chain runs: Aristotle teaches Alexander, Alexander spreads Greek civilization east, the Hellenistic synthesis produces the vocabulary that shapes everything downstream. Remove Alexander and the entire chain shifts.

7. He died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged thirty-two. When asked who should inherit his empire, he reportedly said: "The strongest." The empire fragmented. The synthesis project was abandoned. But the Hellenistic world he made lasted three centuries and produced the intellectual environment in which the West was formed. He covered thirty thousand kilometers. He never lost a battle. He carried the civilization that made everything else possible across the known world – and died before he could see what it produced.

Not celebrated enough. Not even close.

Not  AI. This photo was taken in 2016 in Hujialing Village 胡家岭村, Shandong, China.

This seven-story structure went viral for its striking resemblance to Howl’s Moving Castle. 

Built single-handedly by a local villager named Mr. Hu, who has a mental disability, the castle took nearly five years to complete. Using only collected bricks, mud, and salvaged wooden logs—without a single piece of steel or cement—he gathered every material and did all the heavy lifting entirely on his own.

His reason for building it was simple: "So many people built houses, so I wanted to build one too."

Though he never actually lived in it, neighbors grew concerned over its structural safety. The local government eventually coordinated with Mr. Hu to relocate him into a safe, comfortable new home and safely dismantled the structure.

content:
Del traveled to France as part of his "In Search of They" tour, and the interviews he gathered there may be the most significant of his career. The question driving the investigation: who actually coordinated the global COVID response, and how did it happen simultaneously across every nation on earth?

Dr. Louis Fouché, an intensive care physician at Marseille's largest university hospital, achieved 0% COVID mortality in his ward during the first wave by ignoring WHO protocols and treating patients with oxygen, ivermectin, and anti-clotting medication. Hospitals following official protocols reported 30 to 40% lethality. He was called a murderer by superiors, suspended for 606 days without pay while supporting three children, and never once contacted by WHO to ask what he was doing differently. He built an underground network that treated 25,000 patients at home. None of them died.

Professor Christian Perrone ran France's national vaccine committee for roughly 15 years and worked directly with WHO and the Gates Foundation on international vaccine programs. He noticed that two weeks before COVID arrived in France, the Health Ministry moved hydroxychloroquine from over-the-counter to prescription-only. When he said publicly the disease was not as dangerous as portrayed, the government issued a press release forbidding media from interviewing him. TV stations that continued to do so were fined. He describes watching Bill Gates and Gavi systematically colonize WHO over years, subsidizing poor countries' vaccine programs at low prices and raising costs once the vaccines were embedded in national recommendations, making removal politically impossible. A Gates collaborator confirmed the model directly to Perrone on a plane: make the return on investment in rich countries first, then profit from scale in poor countries.

French scientist Guillaume Crépeau closes the segment with 13 years of aluminum adjuvant research showing that immune cells carrying aluminum from vaccines can biopersist for up to 29 years, travel to the brain through the lymphatic system, impair mitochondrial energy production in ways that compound with each injection, and trigger microglial inflammation that can permanently alter brain development, beginning with exposures during pregnancy. Del connects this directly to the Hannah Poling case, the only autism case ever conceded by the federal government, in which vaccines were found to have triggered a pre-existing mitochondrial disorder.

It would be nice if OpenAI was paying me, but I just call things as I see them

I don’t have any delusions about Altman and OpenAI

I think Altman is also a bad person, but in a self-interested way

A garden-variety robber baron, so to speak

And OpenAI is a self interested company seeking to maximize their own financial success

So that is what it is and it’s somewhat predictable

Anthropic is in a different category

They have a clear ideological goal that they are seeking to achieve, which is to get to self improving AGI before anyone else so that they can be the ones who dictate exclusively the future of intelligence on the planet

They may comfort themselves with nice sounding ideas about their good intentions, but such ideologically motivated utopian programs are exactly what has resulted in the worst evil on this planet

The committee for public safety during the French revolution was 100% trying to do what they thought was best for the future of the west, and they ended up chaining children to boats and sinking those boats in front of the parents as they sought to put down the rebellion in the west of France

Even the expression, “you have to break a few eggs to make an omelette,” came from Robespierre

The difference here is the one that CS Lewis points out, a robber baron knows that some level that what they are doing is wrong and they will be limited by that knowledge to some degree

But someone who is completely convinced in the righteousness of their cause has no limits and will never stop inflicting harm on others in the pursuit of their noble goal

That is why I feel that anthropic must lose, and it is important not to support them

content:
ジュニアの資料を見ていて、結構もったいないなと思うのが、「数字と固有名詞の力を、全然借りていない」ということです。

固有名詞って、文章にものすごい力があります。

たとえば、
「複数サービスを横断した顧客基盤を構築している」
より、
「楽天経済圏のように、EC、金融、通信など複数のサービスを横断して顧客接点を持っている」
と書いた方が、一瞬で絵が浮かびます。

「生成AIを活用している」
より、
「Claude Codeを活用している」
と書いた方が、少なくとも生成AIに詳しい人なら、どの程度のものを使っているのか、かなり具体的にイメージできます。

数字も同じです。

「エラーが多発している」
より、
「年間数百件のエラーが発生している」。

「大規模な顧客基盤を持つ」
より、
「国内300万人の会員基盤を持つ」。

「特定チャネルへの依存度が高い」
より、
「売上の約6割を代理店チャネルが占める」。

後者の方が、圧倒的にパワーがあります。

別に、ファーストビュレットで、
「強固な顧客基盤を有する」
「品質面に課題がある」
「独自の経済圏を形成している」
とまとめること自体は、全然悪くありません。

コンサル資料なので、最初に抽象化して結論を書くのはむしろ正しい。

ただ、その下まで全部、
「顧客基盤が強い」
「ブランド力が高い」
「シナジーが見込める」
「競争優位性がある」
で終わったら、
「で、具体的に何がどうすごいの？」
となります。

セカンドビュレット以降には、
固有名詞。
数字。
具体的なサービス名。
具体的な企業名。
特徴的な顧客行動。
その会社ならではの事例。

こういうものを、ガンガン入れた方がいいです。

なぜなら、こういう「具体」には、それ単体で大量の情報が詰まっているからです。

これって、文章をちょっと上手に見せるための小技ではありません。

いかに効率よく、一瞬でイメージを伝えるか、という、コミュニケーションの巧拙そのものであり、忙しいハイレイヤー層にデリバリするのであれば、超必須のスキルですし、AI時代に、なまなましい現場にいる人間が出せる「色」のひとつでもあります。

今どき、AIに、
「A社の強みを整理してください」
と聞けば、「ブランド力」、「顧客基盤」、「技術力」、「シナジー」くらいは、公表事例付きで、いくらでも出てきます。

だからこそ、今のコンサルに必要なのは、抽象語を綺麗に並べる力ではなく、現場で起きていることを5W1Hで解像度高く捉えて言語化する力だと思います。

そして、「強み」「弱み」と抽象的に整理して終わるのではなく、その具体をどうカバーし、どう活かして、実際に勝っていくのかまで具体的に書き下していく。

AI時代だからこそ、そういう「現場の具体」と「戦い方」をつなげる力に、人間の価値が出るのだと思います。

content:
【国はAIを使う。では、国会議員はAIをどこまで理解している？】

これは、かなり大きな話だと思います。

政府は今、

「ガバメントAI 源内」

という生成AIを本格的に導入しています。

2026年度中には、

約18万人の政府職員が使えるようにする予定です。

しかも、

法制度を調べるAI。
国会答弁を検索するAI。
さらには「国会答弁を作るAI」まで開発中です。
つまりこれから、
私たちが役所から受け取る情報や、
国会で大臣が答える文章の裏側にも、

AIが普通に入ってくる可能性があります。

私はAIを使うこと自体には賛成です。
人手不足もある。
仕事が速くなる。
調査も効率化できる。

使えるものは使えばいいと思います。

ただ、一つ疑問があります。

AIには、
誤った回答。
著作権。
個人情報。
ディープフェイク。
偏った情報。
いろいろな問題もあります。

そのルールを決めるのは政治です。

日本では2025年に「AI法」も成立しました。

では、

その法律を作り、これからAIのルールを決めていく国会議員は、AIをどこまで理解しているのでしょうか。
ChatGPTを実際に使ったことがあるのか。
生成AIと普通の検索の違いを理解しているのか。
ディープフェイクの危険性をどこまで議論しているのか。
国会議員マップには、議員の国会発言データがあります。

そこで今後、

「生成AI」
「ChatGPT」
「ディープフェイク」
「AI規制」

について、

誰が国会で何を話してきたのかも調べてみたいと思います。

AIは、ものすごい速さで進んでいます。

政府も18万人規模で使おうとしている。

それなら、

ルールを作る側だけが、その速さについていけていない。

そんなことだけは、あってほしくない。

「AIを活用します」

という言葉だけではなく、
そのAIを本当に理解した上で政治をしているのか。
そこも、これから見ていく必要があると思います。
皆さんは、
政治家にどの程度のAI知識が必要だと思いますか？

【出典】
・デジタル庁「ガバメントAI 源内」
・内閣府「AI法」
・内閣府「人工知能基本計画」
